blocks.text: Why would forgiveness involve the cross?
Christ willingly bore the judgment our sins deserve.

God is holy and just, and our sin deserves judgment. In love, the Father sent the Son, who willingly offered himself as our substitute. Christ bore the penalty of sin and satisfied divine justice, reconciling his people to God. This is penal substitution, central to the Reformed account of the cross.
Ligonier MinistriesChrist bearing the penalty of sin
From the claim to the conclusion.
Sin is guilt before God, not merely a feeling of shame or a lack of fulfilment.
The sinless Christ bears our sins; his death is a willing gift.
Through Christ's blood God justifies sinners while remaining just.
Forgiveness rests on Christ's completed obedience and sacrifice, not on God overlooking evil or our paying him back.
One saving work, several biblical descriptions
Scripture also describes ransom, reconciliation and victory. These belong with Christ's bearing our guilt. We should not use one image to remove another part of what the Bible teaches.
Ligonier MinistriesBiblical descriptions of the atonement
The cross is not an unwilling stranger punished by a hostile deity. The incarnate Son freely lays down his life in obedience to the Father. God's love and God's justice meet in this saving work.
Why can't God simply ignore the offence?
The gospel does not deny the seriousness of guilt. God condemns sin and grants mercy through Christ's sacrifice. The righteousness by which we stand before God is Christ's, received through faith.
John CalvinInstitutes III.11: forgiveness and imputed righteousness
A courtroom or debt analogy is an aid to explanation, not a replacement for Scripture's account of the person and work of the mediator.
What would forgiveness mean if God took both the evil of our sin and the cost of our rescue seriously?
